content.text: Physics is the study of the natural world, and to describe it accurately we need to measure things. A
is any property that can be measured and expressed as a number with a unit. Understanding physical quantities and their units is fundamental to all of physics.
Every measurement in physics must include both a number and a unit. Writing '5' on its own is meaningless -- you must specify '5 metres', '5 seconds', or whatever quantity you are measuring.

attrs.title: SI Base Units at a Glance

content.text: Many units are combinations of base units:
Prefixes are used to express very large or very small quantities:

The SI system has seven base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela). All other units in physics are derived from combinations of these base units. For example, the newton (N) is equivalent to kg·m/s².
To convert between units, multiply or divide by the appropriate factor:
Very large or small numbers are written in standard form:
Express 0.000025 m in standard form and convert to micrometres.

When converting units, students often multiply when they should divide, or vice versa. Remember: converting to a smaller unit means the number gets bigger (e.g. 2.5 km = 2500 m), and converting to a larger unit means the number gets smaller (e.g. 450 mm = 0.45 m).
All non-zero digits are significant: 123 has 3 s.f.
Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: 102 has 3 s.f.
Leading zeros are not significant: 0.0025 has 2 s.f.
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 2.50 has 3 s.f.
Your answer should have the same number of significant figures as the least precise measurement used.

Physical quantities have a numerical value and a unit
SI units provide a standardised measurement system
The seven base SI units are: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela
Prefixes (kilo, milli, micro, etc.) express large and small quantities
Significant figures indicate the precision of a measurement
